## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Pilindavaccha Sutta* is the sixth discourse of the *Nandavagga*, the third chapter of the *Udāna* (Ud 3.6, PTS Ud 28) [SuttaCentral; Masefield 1997]. In this sutta, monks complain to the Buddha that the elder Pilindavaccha repeatedly addresses his fellow monastics with terms reserved for outcastes or menials (*vasalavāda*) [Masefield 1997; Jetjiravat]. The Buddha summons Pilindavaccha and inquires into his conduct, then reflects on his former existences and explains to the assembly that Pilindavaccha—despite having attained arahantship—acted entirely without malice; his manner of speaking was merely an ingrained habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) persisting from having been reborn in a brāhman family for five hundred consecutive lifetimes [SuttaCentral; Jetjiravat; Masefield 1997].

SuttaCentral identifies passage-level verse parallels in the *Brāhmaṇavarga* of the Sanskrit *Udānavarga* (UVS 33 / UV 33), its Tibetan version (*The Brāhmaṇa*, Uv Kg 33), and Chinese translations in the *Chuyào jīng* (T 212.34) and *Fǎjí yàosòng jīng* (T 213.33) [SuttaCentral]. It also notes a resembling passage in the *Pūraḷāsa Sutta* (Snp 3.4) and a mention in the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 1) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus matches substantial portions of the text with internal Pali discourses, including the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Bhikkhu Saṁyutta* (SN 21), *Saṁghabhedakakkhandhaka* (Kd 17), *Bhaddiya Sutta* (Ud 2.10), *Nanda Sutta* (Ud 3.2), and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, DharmaNexus automatically aligns the sutta with passages in the Chinese Āgamas—namely the *Biéyì zá āhán jīng* (T 100), *Zhōng āhán jīng* (T 26), *Zá āhán jīng* (T 99), and *Zēngyī āhán jīng* (T 125)—as well as a Tibetan Kangyur text [DharmaNexus].

Modern English translations include those by Peter Masefield and Bhikkhu Sujato, alongside at least 17 translations into 13 languages cataloged by SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral; Masefield 1997].
